name: Non-defining relative clauses; whose, where, when, which
subtitle: A non-defining relative clause adds extra information between commas: My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a nurse. Use which for a whole clause: He was late, which annoyed everyone.
source: icanspeak Spanish original English text (grammar-b2 run, 2026-10-29)

flow.text: noun, + who / which / whose / where / when

concept.exampleHtml: My sister, who lives in Leeds, is a nurse. — He was late, which annoyed everyone.

qa.html: A non-defining relative clause adds extra information. We already know which person or thing we mean. Without the clause, the sentence still makes sense. Put the clause between commas: Tom, who lives next door, is a nurse. The museum, which opened in 1990, is free. A defining clause has no commas: The man who lives next door is a nurse.

Use who for people and which for things. In a non-defining clause you can not use that, and you can not leave out the pronoun. ✗ My phone, that I bought in May, is broken. → ✓ My phone, which I bought in May, is broken.
whose shows that something belongs to the person or thing before it. A noun follows whose: Tom, whose car broke down, was late. The hotel, whose rooms are small, is very cheap.
where is for places and when is for times. We stayed in Bath, where my aunt lives. We arrive on Friday, when the festival starts. After where and when comes a full clause with its own subject.

which can also refer to a whole clause. Then it means "and this". He was late, which annoyed everyone. She passed the exam, which surprised us. There is always a comma before it, and you cannot use that or what here.

what means "the thing that". It has no noun before it: What I need is a holiday. I don't understand what you mean. After everything, something, nothing, all use that: ✗ everything what he said → ✓ everything that he said.

Typical mistakes: ✗ My bike, that I bought last year, is broken. → ✓ My bike, which I bought last year, is broken. · ✗ She passed, what surprised us. → ✓ She passed, which surprised us. · ✗ The film, which I saw it on Friday, was long. → ✓ The film, which I saw on Friday, was long. (no extra it)

concept.noteHtml: In speech, a non-defining clause has short pauses where the commas are. In formal writing you may also see whom after a preposition (Dr Evans, with whom I work), but who is normal in everyday English. For defining clauses (no commas, that is possible), see Relative clauses. For prepositions at the end of a clause (the friend I travelled with), see Prepositions at the end.

listen.text: My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a nurse.
listen.note: A non-defining clause: extra information between commas, with who.

listen.text: We stayed in Bath, where my aunt lives.
listen.note: Where for a place. A full clause follows.

listen.text: He was late, which annoyed everyone.
listen.note: Which refers to the whole first part: he was late.

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose the words you hear. Listen for who, which, whose, where, when and what.

items.text: Tom, whose car broke down, was late.
We stayed in Bath, where my aunt lives.
He was late, which annoyed everyone.
What I need is a holiday.
The museum, which opened in 1990, is free.
We arrive on Friday, when the festival starts.

rounds.label: 1 · who and which with commas
rounds.instruction: You hear two sentences. Make one sentence. The second sentence becomes extra information between commas.

example.prompt: Tom is my neighbour. He plays the drums.
example.answer: Tom, who plays the drums, is my neighbour.

items.prompt: Amira is my cousin. She lives in Rome.
items.answer: Amira, who lives in Rome, is my cousin.

items.prompt: The museum is free. It opened in 1990.
items.answer: The museum, which opened in 1990, is free.

items.prompt: My laptop is broken. I bought it last year.
items.answer: My laptop, which I bought last year, is broken.

items.prompt: Kwame is a chef. He works in Bristol.
items.answer: Kwame, who works in Bristol, is a chef.

items.prompt: The film was long. We saw it on Friday.
items.answer: The film, which we saw on Friday, was long.

items.prompt: Our teacher is very kind. She comes from Ghana.
items.answer: Our teacher, who comes from Ghana, is very kind.

rounds.label: 2 · whose, where, which
rounds.instruction: You hear two sentences. Join them. Her or his means whose. There means where. That means which.

example.prompt: Zofia is a doctor. Her sister lives in Rome.
example.answer: Zofia, whose sister lives in Rome, is a doctor.

items.prompt: We stayed in Bath. My aunt lives there.
items.answer: We stayed in Bath, where my aunt lives.

items.prompt: He was late. That annoyed everyone.
items.answer: He was late, which annoyed everyone.

items.prompt: Liam is a pilot. His wife is a doctor.
items.answer: Liam, whose wife is a doctor, is a pilot.

items.prompt: She passed the test. That surprised us.
items.answer: She passed the test, which surprised us.

items.prompt: We visited York. We met at university there.
items.answer: We visited York, where we met at university.

items.prompt: The train was cancelled. That made me late.
items.answer: The train was cancelled, which made me late.

exercises.title: who, which, whose, where or when?
exercises.hint: What does the clause add information about: a person, a thing, something that belongs to someone, a place, a time or the whole sentence?
exercises.hintHtml: who / whicha person / a thing, or a whole clause (which).whosebelonging to someone: a noun follows.where / whena place / a time, then a full clause.

items.prompt: My cousin Priya, ___ lives in Delhi, is visiting us.
items.why: Priya is a person, and the clause needs a subject: who.

items.prompt: The castle, ___ was built in 1250, is open to visitors.
items.why: A castle is a thing, and you cannot use that between commas: which.

items.prompt: We stayed in Cardiff, ___ my brother studies.
items.why: Cardiff is a place, and a full clause follows: where.

items.prompt: Our neighbour, ___ dog barks all night, is moving away.
items.why: The dog belongs to the neighbour, and a noun follows: whose.

items.prompt: The match was cancelled, ___ made everyone angry.
items.why: It refers to the whole first part, so use which with a comma.

items.prompt: I'll see you in July, ___ the schools are closed.
items.why: July is a time, and a full clause follows: when.

items.prompt: My bike, ___ I bought last year, is already broken.
items.why: A bike is a thing, and between commas you cannot use that: which.

items.prompt: Olga, ___ I work with, is from Poland.
items.why: Olga is a person: who. (Whom is possible in formal writing.)

items.prompt: She won the race, ___ surprised nobody.
items.why: It refers to the whole first part: which.

items.prompt: ___ I need is a long holiday.
items.why: No noun comes before the gap. What means the thing that.

exercises.title: Defining or non-defining?
exercises.hint: Commas show extra information (non-defining). No commas means the clause tells us which one.

rows.term: The man who lives next door is a nurse.
Tom, who lives next door, is a nurse.
The film that we saw was long.
The film, which we saw on Friday, was long.
The woman whose bag was stolen called the police.
Amira, whose bag was stolen, called the police.
I like the café where we met.
We went to Bath, where my aunt lives.

exercises.title: What goes together?
exercises.hint: Tap the first part, then the part that finishes the sentence.

exercises.title: what, which or that?
exercises.hint: Is there a noun or a whole sentence before the gap? Or nothing? And is there a comma?

items.prompt: I don't understand ___ you mean.
items.why: No noun before the gap. What means the thing that.

items.prompt: She said she was ill, ___ was not true.
items.why: It refers to the whole first part, after a comma: which.

items.prompt: ___ surprised me most was the price.
items.why: No noun before the gap. What means the thing that.

items.prompt: He gave me his old laptop, ___ I'm still using.
items.why: A laptop is a thing, and after a comma you cannot use that.

items.prompt: I'll tell you ___ happened.
items.why: No noun before the gap. What means the thing that.

items.prompt: Everything ___ he said was true.
items.why: After everything use that. What is wrong here.

exercises.title: Gap text: A postcard from Bath.
exercises.hint: Think about the word before the gap: a person, a thing, a place, a time, a possession or a whole sentence.

segments.text:
Hi Diego,

Greetings from Bath! We are staying with my aunt,
is a retired teacher. She lives in a flat near the abbey,
is more than 500 years old. We arrived on Friday,
the weather was perfect. Yesterday we visited the Roman Baths,
you can see the old hot springs. Our guide,
jokes were terrible, still made everyone laugh. It rained all afternoon,

was a pity.

See you soon,
Kwame
